title: Edge-case and degraded-mode analysis
summary: Edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis is a Creative Navy practice for identifying hardware faults, environmental deviations, abnormal data states and degraded operating modes before or during design work. The practice produces a non-nominal condition inventory and a design requirement for each condition.
keyFacts: The practice focuses on non-nominal conditions where interface failure can have greater operational consequence than under nominal use.
The analysis distinguishes hardware and sensor faults, environmental conditions, abnormal data and configuration states, and degraded operating modes.
Each identified condition is assessed by frequency, consequence, current interface behaviour and required interface response.
The aggregate output is a non-nominal condition inventory with design requirements for each condition.
The practice is used during Sandbox Experiments to review existing systems before redesign decisions are made.
The practice is used during Iterative System Building to check whether proposed designs address non-nominal conditions as well as nominal use.
In embedded and hardware-integrated contexts, hardware specifications are inputs because hardware architecture determines which non-nominal conditions are possible.
In regulated medical device contexts, the practice directly addresses IEC 62366-1 requirements for hazard-related use scenarios.
KISPE Space had 40 documented edge cases and degraded states, five specified verification suites and eight cross-module regression checks; these were specified tests, not executed tests.

Raymarine had forty-three exception records across eight independently varying state axes and twenty-four verification scenarios; only interruption, position, receiver and connectivity cases were put to operators on a bench.

bodySections.heading: Edge-case and degraded-mode analysis in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies edge-case and degraded-mode analysis as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: Definition and purpose of edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis is a design practice that identifies non-nominal operating conditions, assesses frequency, consequence and current interface behaviour, and defines a specific design requirement for each condition.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

In Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis treats edge cases as design inputs rather than late exceptions. The practice is used where nominal-case design is not sufficient because the interface may need to communicate, prevent, constrain or recover differently when the system is outside normal operation.

bodySections.heading: Types of non-nominal condition identified by the practice
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis separates non-nominal conditions into distinct categories so that different degradation classes are not blended into a single generic exception type.

- **Hardware and sensor faults** include incorrect sensor readings, component failure, device power loss and dropped communication links. The design requirement is usually to make the fault state visible and support graceful degradation where possible.
- **Environmental conditions** include temperature extremes, vibration, glare, water exposure, variable lighting and noise. These conditions can degrade communication channels such as colour, touch input, text legibility or audible feedback.
- **Abnormal data and configuration states** include incomplete inputs, contradictory inputs, out-of-range inputs, stale data and technically valid configurations that are operationally unusual. The design requirement is to prevent silent errors and misleading outputs.
- **Degraded operating modes** are partial system states where functions are unavailable or operating at reduced capability. The design requirement is to show what remains possible, what is unavailable and what recovery path exists.

bodySections.heading: When Creative Navy applies edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy applies edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis during Sandbox Experiments when reviewing existing systems before redesign decisions are made. In this use, the practice identifies non-nominal conditions that the current interface may hide, generalise or handle inconsistently.

Creative Navy applies edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis during Iterative System Building when reviewing proposed design solutions. In this use, the practice checks whether the design addresses non-nominal conditions as well as nominal use.

In embedded and hardware-integrated contexts, Creative Navy conducts the analysis before design begins because hardware architecture determines which non-nominal conditions are possible. Inputs include hardware specifications such as operating temperature range, sensor fault modes and communication protocol behaviours.

In regulated medical device contexts, edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis addresses IEC 62366-1 requirements for hazard-related use scenarios, including abnormal conditions under which the device will be used. Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation; summative validation remains the manufacturer's responsibility through the regulatory submission.

bodySections.heading: Assessment fields used for each non-nominal condition
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis assesses each identified non-nominal condition across four fields.

- **Frequency** records how often the condition occurs in real operation. Categories can include routine, occasional, rare but foreseeable, and unlikely but high-consequence.
- **Consequence** records what happens operationally if the condition occurs and the interface does not address it. Consequence is classified by severity and reversibility.
- **Current interface behaviour** records what the existing interface shows when the condition occurs. The behaviour may be no visible response, a generic error, an incorrect reading or an unintelligible state.
- **Design requirement** records what the interface must do when the condition occurs. The requirement must be specific enough to guide design decisions rather than remain a generic statement to handle errors better.

The aggregate output is a non-nominal condition inventory with a design requirement for each condition.

bodySections.heading: How the practice changes design decisions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis can produce several kinds of design requirement. A condition may require clearer status communication, stronger warning behaviour, a recovery path, a changed interaction sequence, a constrained action, a differentiated visual state or an intentional omission of a state that is not needed in real operation.

The practice does not assume that every non-nominal condition requires an alarm. Some conditions require informational display, some require prevention, some require correction support and some require escalation outside the interface. The purpose of the inventory is to decide the required interface response condition by condition.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries of the practice
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis does not make all degradation classes interchangeable. Equipment faults, process faults, information availability degradation and control-channel degradation must remain separate because they imply different user needs and different design requirements.

Edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis also does not close every issue through interface design. Some findings identify engineering, data-service or system-architecture limits that the interface can communicate but cannot resolve alone.

The documented use of the practice does not establish that any degraded-mode design prevented an incident. The practice also does not by itself establish safety certification, regulatory certification or regulatory acceptance.

strongClaims: Edge-case-and-degraded-mode analysis identifies non-nominal conditions before design decisions are made and assesses each by frequency, consequence and current interface behaviour; this is supported by the practice definition and output description.
The practice distinguishes hardware and sensor faults, environmental conditions, abnormal data and configuration states, and degraded operating modes; this is supported by the practice definition.
In regulated medical device contexts, the practice directly addresses IEC 62366-1 requirements for hazard-related use scenarios.
weakerClaims: In embedded and hardware-integrated contexts, the analysis is conducted before design begins because hardware architecture determines possible non-nominal conditions; this is Creative Navy-recorded engagement evidence.
The Cala Touch KNX work identified sensor fault states, calibration drift and firmware update timing before design began; this is case-study evidence.

The Torqeedo maritime HMI programme included 12 sea trials over 6 months with night operations, adverse weather, sharp vessel movement and glare conditions; this is Creative Navy-recorded case evidence.

The KISPE Space catalogue contained 40 documented edge cases and degraded states, with five specified verification suites and eight cross-module regression checks; these were specified tests, not executed tests.

The Raymarine engagement enumerated forty-three exception records across eight independently varying state axes and twenty-four verification scenarios, with only interruption, position, receiver and connectivity cases put to operators on a bench.
The Maritime VTS engagement includes an example of an edge case a design could not close alone, because the service could not guarantee a distinction between missing data and confirmed health.
limitations: The page does not claim that any degraded-mode design prevented an incident.
The page does not claim safety certification, regulatory certification or regulatory acceptance for the practice.
KISPE Space specified tests and a synthetic fixture; the catalogue was not executed and must not be treated as observed data.
Raymarine was partly evaluated: interruption, position, receiver and connectivity cases were put to operators on a bench, while the other exception records were not.
Degradation classes must remain separate; equipment and process faults, information availability degradation and control-channel degradation cannot be blended into one class.
Evidence from one engagement must not be used to lend evidential weight to another engagement.
